value.overview: The Russet-naped Wood-Rail is a large, colorful rail of wetlands, damp woodland, and forest edges in Middle America. It has a gray head and neck, a conspicuous russet patch on the back of the head, a warm brown breast, dark lower underparts, a long yellowish bill, and pinkish legs. Although rails are often secretive, this species may walk openly along streams, ponds, marsh edges, and muddy banks, usually alone or in pairs.
value.classification: It belongs to the rail family, Rallidae, and the genus Aramides. It was formerly treated as a subspecies of the Gray-necked Wood-Rail, Aramides cajaneus, but is now generally recognized as a separate species.
value.identification: This chicken-sized rail has olive-brown upperparts, a gray head and neck, and a bright reddish-brown or russet patch on the rear crown and nape. The breast and flanks are warm cinnamon or rufous, while the belly, undertail, and tail are blackish. Its long bill is yellowish, the eyes are red, and the legs are pink to reddish. In Costa Rica, voice and range are useful because it can overlap with the Gray-cowled Wood-Rail.
value.rangeHabitat: The Russet-naped Wood-Rail occurs from Mexico through parts of Central America to northeastern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is chiefly associated with the Caribbean lowlands and foothills, including the northeastern part of the country, where the subspecies plumbeicollis is reported. It uses freshwater marshes, swamp forest, river and stream margins, mangroves, tropical dry or thorn forest, semi-evergreen forest, and dense vegetation near wetlands. It generally requires thick cover close to water.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, birds are present as resident breeders, especially in suitable habitat in the northeastern Caribbean region; seasonal movements within the country may occur but are not well documented.
value.breeding: The nesting season is incompletely known. Breeding-condition adults have been recorded in January, April through June, and August, suggesting that nesting may occur during several periods and may be influenced by local rainfall. The nest is a shallow, loosely built bowl made from sticks and plant fibers. It is placed in a bush, tangle of vines, or small tree, sometimes a few meters above the ground. Both adults are believed to remain near the nest and young.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet is not known in detail, but documented foods include plant material, snails, crabs, and at least one snake. The bird usually forages on foot in dense vegetation, wet leaf litter, and along stream or pond margins. It may also feed in grassy openings near forest and can walk in the open while probing or picking food from the ground. Its long bill is useful for handling a varied mixture of animal and plant foods.
value.behavior: The Russet-naped Wood-Rail is usually secretive, but it can be surprisingly bold and visible along water edges. It commonly occurs singly or in pairs and walks rather than flying when moving through suitable habitat. Individuals often keep close to dense vegetation, where they can retreat quickly if disturbed. Calls are loud and distinctive for a rail, and vocal activity may make the species easier to detect than its subdued movement and habitat preferences would suggest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is not currently recognized as undergoing a meaningful range-wide decline. In Costa Rica, its status is best understood through continued monitoring of Caribbean lowland wetlands, waterways, and forest cover.
